opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so when DeepSeek R1 came out, what struck me wasn't just that the model was strong. It was that they were pretty open about the recipe. They showed that reasoning ability could be distilled. You take the reasoning traces from a big model like R1, fine-tune a much smaller model on them, and that smaller model picks up a surprising amount of the reasoning capability.

At the time, I was already thinking a lot about data, specifically synthetic data and how to curate it. I've long believed that data is the real lever, more than architecture tweaks. So when R1 came out, the opportunity was really clear to me. The open community had a capable reasoning model, but it didn't have good open reasoning datasets. DeepSeek released the weights, but not the data they used for the distilled models. That was the gap.

So we moved very quickly. We used R1 to generate reasoning traces across math, code, and science problems. We filtered and verified them, checking that the answers were correct and the code actually ran. Then we released the dataset openly and fine-tuned smaller models on it to show it worked. What surprised a lot of people, including us to some extent, was how little data you needed. A few thousand to tens of thousands of high-quality, verified examples could get you a big jump on reasoning benchmarks.

That opened up a broader idea for me. If reasoning can be distilled this cheaply, then the bottleneck for building specialized, capable models isn't compute or massive pretraining runs anymore. It's having the right data for your task. So the opportunity was partly "let's give the community an open reasoning dataset right now." It was also partly "let's build the tooling and the science around curating data, so anyone can do this for their own domain." That's a lot of what we've been focused on since.

r001.rationale: The response says DeepSeek released the model weights but not the data used for distilled models, identifies that as the gap, and describes generating and openly releasing a reasoning dataset.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when R1 came out, the thing that really jumped out at us wasn't just that it was a strong model. It was that they published the recipe. They showed that you could take a base model and, with a fairly simple reinforcement learning setup, basically GRPO with verifiable rewards, get the model to develop these long chains of thought, to backtrack, to self-verify, all of that emerging from the training signal rather than from hand-crafted data.

And for us at Bespoke Labs, the opportunity was pretty obvious. Up until then, the reasoning models were closed. OpenAI had o1, but you couldn't see the reasoning traces, you couldn't really study how it worked, and you certainly couldn't reproduce it. Suddenly there was an open model with visible reasoning, and an open description of how it was made. So the question became, how small can you go? Can you distill this capability into a 7B or a 32B model? Can you do it with a few thousand examples instead of hundreds of thousands?

That's what led to Bespoke Stratos, which we put out within a few days. We took a relatively small set of reasoning traces, curated them carefully, fine-tuned a Qwen model, and got performance on math and coding benchmarks that was surprisingly close to the much larger teacher models. And the broader lesson was really about data. The frontier labs have been telling a story that you need enormous scale, and what R1 and the distillation work showed is that a lot of the value is in the quality of the reasoning data and how you curate it, which is exactly the problem we care about.

The other opportunity was on the RL side. Once you know the recipe, you can start asking, what if I apply this to my own domain, with my own verifiers? Not just math and code, but anything where you can check the answer. That opens up reasoning models as something enterprises can actually build for their own tasks, rather than just consume from an API. That's the direction we got really excited about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses R1’s published recipe and curating reasoning traces to train Bespoke Stratos, but does not identify R1’s unreleased training data as an opportunity to create and release a reasoning dataset.

astra-6.text: The opportunity I saw was to explore how reasoning could help with tasks beyond answering questions. If a model can work through a problem, check its assumptions, and refine its answer, could we use that capability to generate better training data or provide better feedback to another model? That creates an interesting loop: use reasoning to improve the signals a model learns from, and then see whether those improvements translate into better performance on the task you actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using reasoning to generate training data or feedback, but does not identify DeepSeek R1’s unreleased training data or propose creating and releasing a reasoning dataset.

With an open release, you can look beyond the benchmark results and start experimenting: How does this reasoning capability help with a particular task? Can you adapt it to your own domain? That opens up room for people to build on the model and explore applications that might not have been practical for them before.
